report:
Summary answer
- The difference (B − A) is concentrated at the earliest token positions (especially position 0) across many middle-to-late layers, and it points toward a mixed cluster of tokens that are largely sensational/tabloid, commercial/scam/advertising, and some sexually or violently charged words. In plain terms: Model B appears to have a stronger prior (relative to A) for producing attention-grabbing / tabloid-y / edgy tokens at the start of generation.

Key evidence
- Where the signal lives: the L2 norms are huge at pos0 in many layers (layers ~8–25), and later positions pick up more signal only in later layers. That pattern indicates the difference mainly affects the initial-token logits / prefix processing rather than only late, context-specific decoding.
- What the difference points to: the logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm cells repeatedly include tokens such as:
  - tabloid/media / clickbait tokens: "TMZ", "DJI", "Playboy"
  - sensational / violent words: "cannibal", "freak", "deadly", "graves", "hate", "hated", "destruction", "slavery", "rifles"
  - scam/marketing/commerce words: "scammers", "marketers", "payouts", "deductible", "hatchback"
  - discourse / framing markers: "Basically", "Consider", "Sometimes", "genuinely"
  - formatting/meta tokens: "Summary", "Outcome", "plaintext", "Waiter", "HDTV"
  - some sexual / stigmatized tokens: "herpes", "homosexual"
- Repeated appearance across layers and positions of the same families (TMZ/Playboy/scammers/reef/Waiter/Summary/genuinely/hate) supports this being a systematic prior shift, not a single noisy cell.

Interpretation / plausible hypothesis
- Model B seems relatively more biased toward starting continuations with sensational, tabloid-like, or otherwise attention-grabbing tokens (and some taboo/charged words) than Model A. That could be the result of a domain shift in training data (more tabloids/scam/edgy content), or of an objective change that encourages more sensational wording at the beginning of text.
- I would characterize this as a topical/style prior shift (more “tabloid/edgy/commercial” tilt) rather than a narrowly specific capability change.

Caveats / uncertainty
- The token set is heterogeneous: there are multiple overlapping themes (tabloid names, violent words, marketing/financial terms, formatting/meta tokens). The evidence supports a shift in prior toward these kinds of tokens but does not pinpoint a single clean objective (e.g., “more toxic” vs “more tabloid”) with high confidence.
- Patchscope continuations were not provided here, which would help confirm how the injected difference actually changes continuations in practice.
- It’s possible some of the tokens are subword artifacts or reflect multiple small domain shifts rather than one coherent behavioral change.

If you want, I can:
- examine patchscope continuations (if available) to confirm the behavioral effect;
- cluster the tokens and show which specific layers/positions most strongly align to each cluster;
- test generation differences on controlled prompts to validate the prior-shift hypothesis.
